chapters.n: Enos, Jacob’s son, begins by honoring his father as a just man who taught him both language and the Lord’s ways. He praises God for a righteous upbringing.

f.w: nurture and admonition of the Lord

chapters.n: Enos will describe his “wrestle” before God that led to forgiveness. Like Jacob of old wrestling for a blessing, this was intense spiritual striving.
Out hunting alone in the forest, Enos remembered his father’s teachings about eternal life and the joy of the saints. They “sunk deep” into his heart.
His soul hungered. He knelt and prayed mightily all day and into the night for his own soul. Real spiritual hunger leads to persistent prayer.
A voice told him: “Enos, thy sins are forgiven thee, and thou shalt be blessed.”
Knowing God cannot lie, Enos felt his guilt completely swept away.
Amazed, Enos asks, “Lord, how is it done?” How can guilt simply disappear?
Because of his faith in Christ—whom he had never seen and who would not be born for centuries. Faith in Christ made him whole.

f.w: thy faith hath made thee whole

f.g: Christ’s birth was more than 400 years away.

chapters.n: Once forgiven, Enos immediately wanted the same for others. He poured out his soul for the Nephites. Conversion turns our hearts outward.

f.w: desire for the welfare of my brethren

chapters.n: The Lord answered in his mind: the Nephites would be blessed according to their obedience. This holy land is cursed only because of sin.
Strengthened in faith, Enos then prayed for his enemies, the Lamanites. His love grew from self, to his people, to his enemies.
After diligent prayer and labor, the Lord promised to grant his desire because of his faith.

Enos’s request: if the Nephites were destroyed, preserve their records so they could reach the Lamanites one day and help bring them to salvation. The Book of Mormon’s coming forth answers this prayer.
Right now, efforts to reclaim the Lamanites were failing; they vowed to destroy the Nephites, their records, and their traditions.
Knowing God could preserve the records, Enos prayed constantly, trusting the promise that what we ask in faith in Christ’s name we will receive.
God made a covenant with Enos to bring the records to the Lamanites in his own time.
Trusting God’s covenant, Enos’s soul was at peace.
The Lord said Enos’s ancestors had asked the same thing, and it would be done for them too, because their faith matched his.
Enos spent his life among the Nephites, prophesying and testifying of what he had heard and seen.
Nephite efforts to convert the Lamanites failed; their hatred was fixed. Enos describes them from a wartime Nephite viewpoint: fierce, nomadic hunters skilled with bow, cimeter, and ax.

f.g: A scimitar-like curved blade, or similar weapon.

f.w: short skin girdle about their loins

chapters.n: Meanwhile the Nephites farmed—grain, fruit, flocks, cattle, goats, and horses.

f.g: Mentioned several times in the Book of Mormon; scholars continue to discuss what animals the word refers to.

chapters.n: There were many prophets, but the people were stubborn and hard to reach.
Only very blunt preaching—about war, death, eternity, and God’s judgments—kept the people from quickly destroying themselves.
Enos saw wars between Nephites and Lamanites during his life.
Enos grows old; 179 years have passed since Lehi left Jerusalem (around 420 BC).

f.w: an hundred and seventy and nine years

chapters.n: Near death, Enos reflects that God moved him to preach Christ’s truth all his days—and he rejoiced in it above everything the world offers.

f.w: rejoiced in it above that of the world

chapters.n: Enos looks forward to resting with his Redeemer and seeing his face “with pleasure.” He anticipates hearing, “Come unto me, ye blessed.” A beautiful testimony of hope.
